title: Japan Struggles to Respond to Cascade of Data Leaks
paragraphs: Japan is facing a growing wave of cyberattacks that has exposed the personal information of millions of people, and the government is struggling to respond.

In recent weeks, more than 20 major Japanese companies have disclosed that they were attacked. One of the most serious cases involved Times Car, a car-sharing service. In October 2026, an attack leaked information from about 6.6 million member accounts, including images of driver's licenses. Meanwhile, the railway company JR East lost the email addresses of 1.67 million customers, and Lawson, Daiwa Securities and Bookoff also reported leaks of customer data.

In another case, IDC Frontier, a cloud services company owned by SoftBank, was hit by a ransomware attack on October 7. The outage affected 495 companies and local governments. For example, it stopped the logistics system of Nissui Logistics at 17 sites and took the websites of Ibaraki Prefecture offline.

The problem has been growing for some time. According to the National Police Agency, there were a record 123 ransomware incidents in the first half of 2026. Masaaki Taira, a senior member of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party, described the situation as a state of emergency in cyberspace.

The government has taken several steps. The Financial Services Agency told banks to accept only identity documents that contain chips, such as passports and My Number cards, because images of driver's licenses had been leaked. In addition, since October 1, a new law has allowed the government to take action against the tools used by attackers.

On November 6, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi announced an emergency cybersecurity package worth 10 billion yen, or about $63 million. It includes a "cyber rescue team" of public and private experts to help companies that are attacked, as well as a team that will use artificial intelligence to fight hackers and find weaknesses in networks. Takaichi said that a rapid response is essential in an era of AI-generated attacks.

However, experts say there is no firm evidence that AI was used in the recent attacks. Nevertheless, some believe that AI is making attacks much cheaper to carry out. Japan's digital transformation minister, Toshiharu Furukawa, warned that the attacks are becoming increasingly sophisticated.
